title: Why Listening Only to Nearby Opinions Splits a Crowd
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

source.title: Opinion Dynamics and Bounded Confidence: Models, Analysis, and Simulation
source.venue: Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation (JASSS), vol. 5, no. 3

intro.summary: The paper asks when a group of people who keep averaging each other's opinions ends up agreeing, splitting into two camps, or breaking into many small groups. The authors review simple 'everyone averages everyone' models, then study a new rule called bounded confidence: each person only averages the opinions that sit close enough to their own. Computer simulations show three phases. A narrow listening range leaves many opinions, a middle range produces two camps, and a wide range gives consensus. A bias toward one's own side can break a consensus and push the camps to the extremes. These are idealised models explored mostly by simulation, with one-dimensional opinions and everyone able to hear everyone. They are not tested against real survey data, and the authors note that restricting who talks to whom may change the picture.
background: An opinion here is a single number between 0 and 1, like a position on a left–right scale or an expert's estimate.
Older models assumed that people take a weighted average of others' opinions over and over, which usually ends in agreement.
A 'nonlinear' model is one where who influences whom depends on the opinions themselves, so the rules change as opinions move.
When the maths gets too hard, researchers run many computer simulations and look for patterns that hold across runs.
intro.aha: If people simply lean toward listening to their own side, a crowd that would otherwise agree breaks into two camps, and these camps end up at the very extremes rather than in the middle.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Groups sometimes reach agreement, sometimes split into two hostile camps, and sometimes scatter into many small factions. The authors want a simple mathematical account of which of these happens and why. Earlier models almost always predicted agreement, which does not match the splits seen in real communities.
primer.quote: When does opinion formation within an interacting group lead to consensus, polarization or fragmentation?

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: They first set out the classic model, in which every person repeatedly replaces their opinion with a weighted average of everyone's opinions, and stated its known results. They then studied 'bounded confidence': a person only averages the opinions within a distance ε (epsilon) of their own and ignores everyone further away. This rule is simple, but its maths is hard. So they ran large computer simulations with 625 people starting at random opinions, varying ε and later making the listening window lopsided.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: A small window leaves many surviving opinions. A middle-sized window leaves two camps, and a large window brings everyone together. Polarisation happens because people at the edges are only pulled inward, so they bunch up. These bunches pull in their neighbours until the crowd tears apart, and once torn it never rejoins. When people listen more to their own side, the pull toward the centre fades at the edges, and even a wide window can end in two extreme camps.
primer.quote: More exactly, we step from fragmentation (plurality) over polarisation (polarity) to consensus (conformity).

primer.heading: Why it matters
primer.body: The model shows that two camps can form without anyone being stubborn or extreme to begin with. A mild limit on whom people take seriously is enough. The results come from idealised simulations, not from data on real groups. The authors' first tests suggest that letting people talk only with close neighbours may make polarisation disappear.
primer.quote: Thus, instead of a drive direction centre the opinion based bias generates a drift to the extremes.

concepts.title: Keep averaging and everyone meets in the middle
concepts.idea: When every person repeatedly replaces their opinion with the average of everyone's opinions, the spread of opinions shrinks until all agree.

predict.question: A new case with unequal trust. Ann listens only to herself. Ben and Cara each give half their trust to themselves and half to Ann. Nobody else is involved. After many rounds of updating, what happens?
options: All three end up at Ann's starting opinion
All three meet at the average of their three starting opinions
Ben and Cara agree with each other, but Ann stays apart
They never agree, because Ann refuses to listen
why: Right. Ann never moves, and each round Ben and Cara halve their gap to her. Every pair shares trust in Ann, so the paper's condition for agreement holds, and she sets the meeting point.
Tempting, since equal trust gave the plain average. But the meeting point depends on who trusts whom, and here all trust flows to Ann.
That would need Ben and Cara to listen only to each other. Both listen to Ann, who never moves, so both are pulled all the way to her.
One stubborn person doesn't block agreement; she fixes where it lands. The paper only asks that any two people share trust in some third, and everyone trusts Ann.

terms.means: An average where each opinion is counted with its own share of trust, and the shares add up to 1
How much one person counts another person's opinion when forming their own
Everyone in the group holding the same opinion

model.title: A crowd that talks in rounds
model.note: Teaching model: the paper's averaging rule in its simplest case. With the switch on, every person gives equal weight to everyone. The paper's classical model also allows unequal weights, which make agreement arrive gradually rather than in one round. With the switch off, each person listens only to opinions within 0.01 of their own. That is the simulation's narrowest setting, standing in for 'listen only to yourself'. Starting opinions are random, and updates happen simultaneously, as in the paper. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

outputs.label: Gap between the two most extreme opinions

steps.say: Here is a crowd of people. Each holds an opinion somewhere on a scale from 0 to 1.
This slider sets how many people are in the crowd.
This one sets how many rounds of talking happen. In each round, everyone updates their opinion at the same moment.
This switch decides who people listen to: everyone, or only those who already think almost exactly as they do.
These two boxes report how far apart the two most extreme people are, and how many separate groups of opinion remain.

explore.prompt: Play with the switch, the rounds and the crowd size. When does talking bring everyone together, and when does it change nothing?

goals.text: Keep the crowd almost as divided as it started, even after a long run of talking.
hints: What has to happen for anyone's opinion to move at all?
If people only hear near-copies of their own view, do extra rounds of talking change much?
Turn the listening switch off, then push the rounds slider well into the upper part of its range.

goals.text: Show that a bigger crowd does not slow agreement: get more than 250 people to full agreement in a single round.
hints: What must every person do for the whole crowd to land on the same number?
Make sure everyone listens to everyone, and bring the rounds slider back to its lowest setting.
Then grow the crowd until it passes the target size, and watch the gap box.

feedback.correct: Yes. Repeated averaging still yields agreement under unequal trust, as long as every pair shares trust in someone. Ann is trusted by all and never moves, so the group closes in on her opinion. The paper notes that which consensus you reach depends on the starting opinions and the weights.
feedback.incorrect: You may have assumed that agreement always lands on the plain average, or that one person who won't budge blocks it. In the paper's classical model, agreement comes whenever any two people both put some weight on a common third person. Here that person is Ann. She never moves, so the others are pulled all the way to her.

steps.say: Start with nobody really listening: each person hears only opinions almost identical to their own. After one round, the gap between the most extreme people is still close to the full scale.
Let them talk for twenty rounds. The crowd barely changes: with no one to listen to, repeating the process does almost nothing.
Now flip the switch so that everyone listens to everyone. Each person replaces their opinion with the average of all opinions, and after a single round the gap is zero.

This is the classical model of opinion formation. Each person forms a weighted average: they give every other person a weight, a share of trust, and the shares add up to 1. Here every weight is equal, one share per person.
Does a bigger crowd take longer? Double it. Everyone still holds the same opinion after one round, because each person averages the very same list of opinions.
Everyone sharing one opinion is called consensus. Only one opinion group is left, and it sits at the crowd's starting average.
With unequal weights, the gap would shrink round by round instead of all at once. The paper proves consensus still comes, as long as any two people both give some weight to a common third person.

understand.explanation: In the classical model, each person's new opinion is a weighted average of everyone's current opinions, and this repeats round after round. An average always lies between the most extreme opinions, so the gap between them can only shrink. When everyone listens to everyone, the gap shrinks to nothing and the group reaches consensus: in one round with equal weights, as in the model, or gradually with unequal weights. The paper proves (Result 1) that consensus comes from every starting point whenever any two people both give weight to a common third, and that where it lands depends on where they started. If everyone sticks to their own view, nothing ever changes. This is a property of a mathematical model, not a measured fact about real groups, and the rest of the paper shows how easily it breaks.
understand.quote: If any two agents put jointly a positive weight on a third one then for every initial opinion profile a consensus will be approached (which consensus, of course, depends on the initial profile).

connect.caption: The paper's equation (2.1). Person i's opinion in the next round (t + 1, the rounds slider) is a weighted average of all n current opinions (n, the crowd size). The weights a_{ij} say how much i trusts j and add up to 1. With the switch on, every a_{ij} equals 1/n. With it off, nearly all of a person's weight sits on themselves, which the paper notes gives no consensus.

concepts.recap: Repeatedly averaging opinions that everyone listens to shrinks the spread until all agree. Where they agree depends on where they started and whom they trust.

concepts.title: A listening window: many groups, two camps, or one
concepts.idea: If people only average opinions within a distance ε of their own, small ε leaves many groups, middle ε leaves two camps, and large ε gives consensus.

predict.question: Take the middle-sized window that split the full crowd into two camps. Now start a different crowd whose opinions all lie in a narrow band, from 0.4 to 0.6, instead of across the whole scale from 0 to 1. Everyone uses that same window. What is the most likely ending?
options: One group: a consensus
Two camps again, as before
Many small groups
Nobody moves at all
why: Right. What matters is how wide the window is compared with the spread of opinions. In a band only 0.2 wide, a window of about 0.15 on each side reaches across most of the crowd. Chains of overlapping listeners pull everyone together.

It is tempting to think a window size always gives the same outcome. But 'middle-sized' only means middle-sized relative to the spread. Here the window covers most of the band, which puts this crowd in the consensus zone.
Many groups appear when the window is small compared with the spread of opinions. Squeezing the opinions together makes the window relatively larger, not smaller.
People stop moving only when nobody else is inside their window. In this band almost everyone has many neighbours within reach, so they keep averaging.

terms.means: How far from your own opinion, on either side, you are still willing to listen. The paper writes it as ε
The rule that each person averages only the opinions inside their confidence level and ignores the rest
The ending where many separate opinion groups survive (the paper also calls it plurality)
The ending where the crowd settles into two opposing camps (the paper also calls it polarity)

model.title: A crowd that only listens to nearby opinions
model.note: Teaching model: the paper's bounded-confidence rule (Hegselmann–Krause). Each round, everyone at once moves to the plain average of all opinions within the listening distance of their own, as in the paper's simulations with a symmetric window that is the same for everyone. Starting opinions are random and uniform, as in the paper, but there are far fewer people than the paper's 625 and only one random start, whereas the paper averaged 50 runs. The group counter treats opinions closer than 0.1 as one group, so at the narrowest windows it can undercount; the picture shows the true clusters. With the switch on, everyone listens to everyone and the slider is ignored. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: How far each person listens (either side)

outputs.label: Gap between the two most extreme opinions

steps.say: Same crowd as before. Each dot is a person, its height is their opinion from 0 to 1, and the rounds of talking run left to right.

The 'everyone listens to everyone' switch is now off. The new slider sets how far each person listens. They average only the opinions within that distance above or below their own, and ignore everyone further away.
Watch the group count as people's reach gets shorter.

explore.prompt: Slide the listening distance back and forth and hunt for the boundaries between the three kinds of ending.

goals.text: Make the crowd end in at least four separate opinion groups
hints: Does a shorter or a longer reach leave more groups behind?
Shrink the listening distance well below the point where two camps appeared.
Look between the narrowest setting and about a tenth of the scale.

goals.text: Find a middle-sized reach where the crowd ends in just two or three camps: not many groups, not one
hints: Consensus lives at the wide end and many groups at the narrow end. The camps are in between.
Start from the consensus setting and narrow the reach a little at a time, watching the group count.
The two-camp zone sits somewhere between a tenth and a fifth of the scale.

feedback.correct: Yes. The outcome depends on the window compared with how spread out the opinions are. A window that splits a crowd spread over 0 to 1 covers most of a crowd squeezed into 0.4 to 0.6, so that crowd reaches consensus.
feedback.incorrect: You probably treated a window size as fixing the outcome on its own. In the bounded-confidence model, what counts is how far the window reaches compared with the spread of opinions. Squeeze the opinions into a narrow band and the same window behaves like a wide one, which leads to consensus.

steps.say: Start with a long reach: each person listens to anyone within 0.4 of their own view. This distance is what the paper calls the confidence level, written ε. Averaging only inside it is called bounded confidence.
With a reach this long, chains of overlapping listeners link the whole crowd. They end in one group: consensus, just as when everyone listened to everyone.
Lower the confidence level to 0.3. Still one group, and the gap between the extremes still closes.
Now the narrow end: 0.07. Most people hear only a handful of others, so small local groups form and stop talking to each other. Many groups survive. The paper calls this fragmentation.
Narrower still, 0.05: even more little groups. Some sit so close together that the counter lumps them as one, but the picture shows them apart.
These groups settle within a few rounds. After that nothing changes, because no group sits inside another's window.

Now the surprise, in the middle: 0.15. Not many groups, not one, but a couple of big camps facing each other. This is polarisation. Why a middle reach makes camps is the puzzle the next concepts open up.

understand.explanation: When people average only the opinions within a distance ε of their own (their confidence level), the size of that window decides how the crowd ends. A very short reach leaves many separate groups. A middle reach usually leaves two camps. A long reach pulls everyone into one consensus. The paper showed this by simulation, not by proof: 625 random opinions, ε stepped from 0.01 to 0.4, and 50 runs at each step. Single runs gave 38 surviving opinions at ε = 0.01, two camps at 0.15 and consensus at 0.25. Individual runs vary, so these phases describe typical outcomes, averaged over many random starting crowds.
understand.quote: Summing up and generalising what we see in Figure 3 one might say: As the homogeneous and symmetric confidence interval increases we transit from phase to phase. More exactly, we step from fragmentation (plurality) over polarisation (polarity) to consensus (conformity)

The set I is the people inside the window and |I| is how many there are. ε is the listening-distance slider and n is the crowd-size slider. concepts.recap: How far people listen sets the ending: a short reach leaves many groups, a middle reach leaves two camps, and a long reach brings consensus.

activities.prompt: The same random crowd, three listening distances. Count the groups in each.
activities.takeaway: One rule, three endings: fragmentation, polarisation, consensus. Only the size of the window changed.

concepts.title: The edges move first, the middle waits
concepts.idea: For an evenly spread crowd, people near the ends see neighbours on only one side, so their average pulls them inward, while people in the middle are pulled equally both ways and at first do not move.

predict.question: A new crowd is spread evenly, but only from 0.2 to 0.8. Nobody holds a view below 0.2 or above 0.8. Everyone listens within a window of 0.1. Who moves in the first round?
options: Everyone moves a little toward 0.5
Only people within 0.1 of the crowd's ends (0.2 and 0.8) move, inward; the rest stay put
Nobody moves, because nobody is near the ends of the scale at 0 and 1
Everyone moves toward the nearer end of the crowd
why: Tempting if averaging feels like a general pull to the centre. But a person whose window holds equal crowds on both sides averages back to their own view, so the middle stays put.

Right. What matters is where the crowd runs out, not where the scale ends. People near 0.2 hear only people above them and move up. People near 0.8 hear only people below and move down. Everyone from 0.3 to 0.7 is balanced and waits.
Tempting if the ends of the scale seem to cause the pull. The pull comes from an empty side of the window. Here the window is empty below 0.2 and above 0.8, so the crowd's own ends move.
Tempting if the edges seem to attract people. The one-sided pull points toward where the neighbours are, which is inward toward the middle of the crowd, never outward.

terms.means: A starting crowd whose neighbouring opinions are all the same distance apart, so it is perfectly evenly spread
Being pulled by neighbours on one side only, because nobody sits on the other side of your window

model.title: How far each person moves in the first round
model.note: Teaching model: an idealised, infinitely large crowd spread perfectly evenly from 0 to 1. This is a smooth version of the paper's evenly spaced start, with a symmetric window and the paper's bounded-confidence rule (everyone averages all views within ε, all at once). Only the first round is shown. With a finite crowd the curve becomes a small staircase, and in later rounds the change spreads inward. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

Share of the crowd that stays put
Marked person's step

steps.say: Picture a crowd spread evenly along an opinion line from 0 to 1. Each spot along the bottom is one person's starting view.
The curve shows how far each person moves after one round of averaging. Above the flat line means moving up; below means moving down.
This slider is the listening window ε from the last lesson. Watch the curve change as it widens.
This slider marks one person. The dot and the box show that person's step.
These boxes show the step of the very last person and the share of the crowd that doesn't move at all.

explore.prompt: Play with the window and the marked person. Can you shape who moves and who waits in round one?

goals.text: Make roughly the middle half of the crowd stay put in the first round
hints: Each end has its own pulled zone. How wide is each one?
Each pulled zone is exactly as wide as the window, and there are two of them, one at each end.
Together the two pulled zones need to cover about half the line, so each one covers about a quarter.

goals.text: Mark the person who starts at 0.30, then find a window just wide enough that this person moves in the first round
hints: This person moves only if their window runs off an edge of the line.
The nearest edge is 0. How far is the person from it?
The window has to reach strictly past 0, so it must be a little wider than this person's distance from 0.

feedback.correct: Yes. The pull comes from an empty side of the window. In this crowd the window is empty below 0.2 and above 0.8, so only people within 0.1 of those ends move, inward. The balanced middle waits.
feedback.incorrect: Averaging does not pull everyone to the centre at once. A person moves only when one side of their window holds fewer people than the other. In an evenly spread crowd that happens only near where the crowd runs out, here at 0.2 and 0.8.

steps.say: Start with a small window. The crowd is perfectly evenly spread, which the paper calls a regular profile. Look at the middle: the curve lies flat on the no-move line.
Why? The person at 0.5 hears everyone from 0.4 to 0.6, with as many people above as below. The average of a balanced window is their own view, so they stay put.

Now mark someone near the bottom at 0.05. Their window would reach down to −0.05, but nobody holds a view below 0. They hear only people above them, so their average sits above them and they move up, toward the centre.
The very last person, at 0, hears only people above and takes the biggest step: half the window. This pull from one side only is what the paper calls one-sided influence.
The top end is the mirror image. People near 1 hear only people below them and move down. Both ends move inward.
Each pulled zone is exactly as wide as the window. Past the line where the window stops touching the edge, the curve goes flat.
Widen the window. The pulled zones grow, the end steps get bigger, and the flat middle shrinks.

Even now, a big block in the middle does not move in round one. It feels the pull only later, after the ends have moved in and changed what the middle hears. Change starts at the edges and travels inward.

understand.explanation: In an evenly spread crowd, a person in the middle has as many neighbours above as below inside their window. Their average equals their own view, so they do not move in the first round. Near an end, the window runs off the opinion line. Nobody sits beyond 0 or 1, so that person hears only people on the inward side, and the average pulls them toward the centre. The pulled zone at each end is exactly as wide as the window, and the very last person moves furthest. The paper showed this with simulations of 50 and 500 evenly spaced opinions at ε = 0.2: changes start at the extremes, reach the centre only after a delay, and the central opinions are the last to move. Our curve shows only the first round of an idealised, infinitely large crowd. The paper also notes that random, uneven starts add bumps in density that can make middle opinions move right away.
understand.quote: From period 0 to 1 nothing changes more in the middle of the opinion space. But as times goes by changes work through the opinion space direction centre. The opinions directly in the centre are the last to be affected.

check.task: Mark a person who is clearly left of centre but who does not move at all in the first round.
check.hint: A person stays put when their whole window fits inside the line, with as many people above as below. Keep them left of centre but out of the pulled zone near 0.
check.misconception: That averaging pulls everyone toward the centre from the first round, so anyone left of centre must move up. In fact only people whose window runs off an edge feel a pull at first.

connect.caption: The paper's bounded-confidence rule (BC): each person's next view is the plain average of everyone within ε, and all update at once. The coloured ε is the window slider. For a crowd spread evenly from 0 to 1, that average is the midpoint of the window clipped to the line. The model's curve, (max(0, x − ε) + min(1, x + ε))/2 − x, is zero where the window fits inside and ε/2 at the very ends. It is the model's version, not a formula in the paper.

concepts.recap: In an evenly spread crowd, only people within ε of an end feel a one-sided pull inward at first; the balanced middle waits until the change works its way in.

concepts.title: From clumps at the edges to a permanent split
concepts.idea: Opinions bunch up at the edges, the bunches pull in nearby opinions, a gap wider than ε opens, and the two sides never influence each other again.

terms.means: Opinions piling up into a dense bunch in one part of the opinion line
A gap between two neighbouring opinions that is wider than ε, so neither listens to the other
The group of opinions on one side of a split, which now changes only from inside itself

concepts.recap: Inward pull at the ends makes dense clumps, the clumps drain the middle, a gap wider than ε opens, and from then on the two sides are cut off for good: that is how two camps form.

understand.explanation: In the last concept the ends of an evenly spread crowd moved inward first while the middle stayed put. If you keep watching, opinions near each end pile up into dense bunches, which the paper calls condensing. A dense bunch acts like a magnet: it pulls in opinions from thinner areas within its listening window ε, so the middle drains toward the two bunches, with opinions above 0.5 moving up and those below 0.5 moving down. In the end two neighbouring opinions sit more than ε apart. That gap is a split, and nobody on one side listens to anyone on the other, not even through a chain of friends, so each side, now a separate sub-profile, settles into its own camp. In the paper's Figure 4 (50 evenly spaced opinions, ε = 0.2) the split appears in period 6. This comes from computer runs of a simple model, not from measuring real people, and random starting opinions add further splits through chance bunching.
understand.quote: In the symmetric case the major causes for polarisation are splits in the opinion profiles. They are caused by shrinking and condensing at the extremes, condensing induced by condensing, and condensing induced by density fluctuations in randomly generated start profiles.

activities.prompt: Follow the paper's reading of Figure 4: 50 opinions, evenly spaced from 0 to 1, everyone with the same window ε = 0.2, all updating at once. Reveal the stages one at a time.

stages.label: 1. Pull from one side
stages.text: People at the very ends have neighbours on only one side, so their average lies toward the centre. They move inward, and the whole range of opinions shrinks.

stages.label: 2. Bunching at the edges
stages.text: Because the end opinions move in faster than their neighbours, they catch up with them. Opinions near each end condense into a dense bunch.

stages.label: 3. Bunches act as magnets
stages.text: A dense bunch weighs heavily in the average of anyone within ε of it. Opinions in thinly populated areas nearby get pulled toward it, which makes the bunch denser still. The paper calls this condensing induced by condensing.

stages.label: 4. The middle drains away
stages.text: The pull finally reaches the centre. Opinions just above 0.5 are drawn upward and those just below 0.5 downward, toward the two bunches. The middle empties out.

stages.label: 5. A gap wider than ε opens
stages.text: In period 6 two neighbouring opinions in the middle end up more than ε apart. That is a split. The two halves are now separate sub-profiles that no longer interact.

stages.label: 6. Two camps settle
stages.text: Each sub-profile keeps averaging only within itself and collapses to one opinion. In the paper's Figure 5, from period 7 to 8 onward nothing changes any more: two camps remain.

activities.takeaway: Polarisation is not built in at the start. It grows step by step from the one-sided pull at the ends, and the split is the moment it becomes permanent.

activities.prompt: Trace the causal route that turns an evenly spread crowd into two permanent camps. Click the boxes in order, following the arrows. Some boxes are tempting dead ends.

nodes.label: Ends see neighbours on one side only
Opinions bunch up at the edges
A gap wider than ε opens
All drift to the overall average

activities.explanation: The chain starts at the ends: one-sided neighbours pull edge opinions inward, they bunch up, the bunches attract nearby opinions, the middle drains toward both bunches, a gap wider than ε opens, and the two sides stop influencing each other. 'Middle opinions move first' is a dead end because the paper shows the centre is the last to be affected: it is pulled equally both ways until the change reaches it. 'All drift to the overall average' is a dead end because that describes everyone listening to everyone. With a middle-sized window the crowd does not end at a single average. It tears into two camps.
hints: Where does movement begin in an evenly spread crowd: at the ends or in the middle?
After the ends move inward, what happens to the density of opinions near them?
The gap comes only after the middle has been emptied toward the two bunches.

activities.question: Once the split has opened, why can the two sides never pull each other back together? Which passage explains this?

options.quote: Under simultaneous updating cracked profiles can never get connected again. Agents/opinions outside ones own sub profile are ‘out of range/reach’ in a quite severe sense: They are not only outside ones own confidence interval, but also outside the confidence intervals of all others one takes seriously, outside the confidence intervals of all others which those others take seriously etc.
options.feedback: Correct. Each person averages only opinions inside their own group, so every new opinion stays inside the range that group already covers. No one inside can reach across the gap, and no chain of 'friends of friends' crosses it either. With nothing pulling the sides together, the gap can only stay open.

options.quote: Extreme opinions are under a one sided influence and move direction centre. As a consequence the range of the profile shrinks.
options.feedback: This is a true passage, but it describes the first stage of the chain: the ends moving inward. It says nothing about what happens after a split, so it cannot explain why split groups stay apart.

options.quote: What irregularity adds are density fluctuations in the initial distribution of opinions. They are additional causes for splits and induce opinion changes deep inside the start–profile without any delay right at the beginning of the process.
options.feedback: This passage is about what causes splits when starting opinions are random: chance bunching creates extra splits early on. It explains how more splits form, not why a split, once formed, never closes.

hints: You want a passage about what happens after the crack, not before it.
Look for the passage that talks about who is in or out of reach, including indirectly.

concepts.title: A lopsided window drags everyone one way
concepts.idea: If everyone looks further to the right than to the left, each person's average sits to their right, so the whole crowd drifts toward the favoured side.

terms.means: A listening window that reaches further on one side of your own opinion than on the other (in the paper, ε_l ≠ ε_r)
The side the window reaches further toward; the crowd drifts that way

model.title: How far each person moves in the first round, with a lopsided window
model.note: Teaching model: the same idealised, perfectly even crowd from 0 to 1. It uses the paper's bounded-confidence rule: everyone averages all views in their window, all at once. The window now reaches ε to the right and only a fraction of ε to the left, the same for every person whatever their opinion. This matches the paper's 'opinion independent' case. Only round one is shown. The paper finds that in later rounds one-sided splits make the drift stronger, and this picture leaves that out. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

predict.question: In a new town the crowd is spread just as evenly and uses the same averaging rule. But everyone looks twice as far to the left as to the right. In round one, what does the crowd's average opinion do?
options: It moves down
It moves up
It stays at 0.5, because the two ends still pull inward
Nothing moves until a gap opens in the crowd
why: Right: now each person's window holds more people below them than above, so their average sits below them. The drift goes to the left, toward the side the window favours.
You may have remembered 'the crowd drifts up' from the walkthrough. The drift follows the tilt, though, and this window leans left, so the crowd goes down.
The ends do still pull inward, but now unevenly: the top is pushed down hard and the bottom only gently. The middle is nudged down too, so the average cannot stay put.
Drift needs no split. In round one the whole middle already moves together, because every window is lopsided. Splits come later and, the paper says, make the drift stronger.

feedback.correct: Yes. The drift follows the tilt. A window that reaches further left puts more people below each person than above, so averages land lower and the crowd moves down. The paper notes that every effect of a right bias has a mirror image for a left bias.
feedback.incorrect: The direction isn't fixed: it comes from which way the window leans. Every person moves toward the side where their window reaches further. With a left-leaning window, the middle and the crowd's average move down.

steps.say: Start with an even window that reaches 0.2 both ways. The middle of the curve lies on the no-move line, because each person there is pulled equally up and down.
Now people look only half as far left as right: 0.1 down, 0.2 up. Each person in the middle now sees more people above them than below.
So their average lands above them. The middle step is half the gap between the two reaches: (0.2 − 0.1)/2 = 0.05. The raised flat stretch is the whole middle moving up together.
Look at the ends. The person at 0 jumps up 0.1, but the person at 1 drops only 0.05. The bottom is pushed up hard, while the top is pulled down only gently.
Add it up and the crowd's average opinion moves up. A window that reaches further one way is called asymmetric confidence, and the side it favours, here the right, is the favoured direction.
Shrink the left reach to a sliver. The middle step nearly doubles and the average climbs further. Little listening in the other direction makes the drift strong.
Now widen the window as well. Almost the whole crowd steps up together. Only a thin strip at the very top still edges down.

understand.explanation: When everyone's window reaches further right than left, each person's average lies above their own opinion, so in an even crowd the whole middle moves up together. The person at the bottom is pushed up hard, while the one at the top is pulled down only a little. The crowd's average therefore moves toward the favoured direction. The paper tested this by walking through many window shapes, with the left reach set to fractions of the right reach, and running 625 random opinions many times at each setting. It found that the final average opinion shifts the way the window leans: strongly when there is little listening in the other direction, more mildly as that listening grows. This picture shows only round one. The paper adds that in later rounds one-sided splits amplify the drift, and that a left-leaning window gives the mirror-image result.
understand.quote: With asymmetric confidence mean and median move into the favoured direction. This effect is extreme if there is only little confidence in the non favoured direction. The effect becomes milder as the confidence in the non favoured direction increases.

connect.caption: The first part is the paper's bounded-confidence rule with a lopsided window (Section 3D). Agent i averages everyone whose opinion lies between ε_l below and ε_r above their own. In the model, ε_r is the ε slider and ε_l is ε times the left-reach slider. The last part is the model's own consequence, not an equation from the paper. In an even crowd, anyone whose window doesn't touch 0 or 1 moves up by half the gap between the two reaches.

concepts.recap: Look further one way than the other and your average lands on that side, so the whole crowd drifts in the favoured direction, most strongly when the other side gets little attention.

concepts.title: Listening to your own side breaks consensus
concepts.idea: When people further right look more to the right and people further left look more to the left (bias slope m), the inward pull at the edges vanishes and the middle drifts outward, so even a wide window can end in two extreme camps.

predict.question: In the paper's runs, a fairly narrow window with no lean left many small groups scattered across the scale. Now give that same narrow-window crowd a strong lean toward their own side. What does the paper report?
options: Still many small groups: with a narrow window, a lean can't change much
Two big camps form, pushed out toward 0 and 1
Everyone ends up agreeing in the middle
The whole crowd slides together toward one end
why: It is tempting to think a narrow window limits everything. But the lean still removes the inward pull at the ends and drags nearby views outward. The paper found that a strong lean produces clear polarisation even with a small window.

Right. The lean stops the ends from moving in, and the outer views pull their neighbours outward. The paper reports that a strong enough lean turns plurality into two camps. With the strongest lean these camps sit at 0 and 1.
Consensus needs a wide window and an inward pull at the ends. Here the window is narrow and the lean removes the inward pull, so agreement becomes even less likely.

That is what a window tilted the same way for everyone does (the previous lesson). Here the window tilts up for people above the middle and down for people below, so the two halves move apart, not together.

terms.means: How strongly each person's window leans toward their own side: 0 means no lean, 1 means the people at the very ends look only outward
A lean in the listening window whose direction depends on where you stand: up for people above the middle, down for people below

model.title: How far each person moves in the first round
model.note: Teaching model: an idealised, infinitely large crowd spread evenly from 0 to 1, a smooth version of the paper's regular profile. It uses the paper's bounded-confidence rule (everyone averages all views inside their window, all at once) with the paper's opinion-dependent lean: the share of the window pointing up is (1−m)/2 + m·x. The ε slider is the reach on each side when there is no lean, so the total window is 2ε; the paper's total window of 0.6 is ε = 0.3 here. Only the first round is shown. The split into camps happens over later rounds, which the paper found by simulation. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

explore.prompt: Recreate the paper's surprise: start from a crowd that ought to agree, then let people lean toward their own side until the ends stop moving in and the middle starts moving out.

goals.text: Choose a window wide enough that the crowd would normally reach consensus, then make the people at the very ends stop being pulled toward the middle.
hints: First make the window wide. Recall how wide it had to be for consensus in the earlier lesson: a bit more than a quarter of the scale on each side.
Then turn up the lean and watch the box for the inward step of the person at either end.
That box shrinks as the lean grows, but it only gets close to zero when the lean slider is almost all the way up.

goals.text: Keep the window wide, place the marked person above the middle, and make them take a clear step away from the middle in round one.
hints: With no lean, a person in the upper half either stays put or is pulled down. What does the lean add?
Turn the lean up strongly, then slide the marked person around the upper half while you watch the step away from the middle.
If the marked person sits too close to the top end, there is little room left above them. Try somewhere between the middle and the top.

feedback.correct: Yes. The lean does not need a wide window to work. It removes the inward pull at the ends and makes outer views attract their neighbours outward. So even a crowd that would have stayed in many small groups gathers into two camps near the extremes.
feedback.incorrect: You may have thought a narrow window, or the lean alone, decides the outcome by itself. The lean changes the direction of the pull at the edges: instead of moving inward, the ends hold still and draw nearby views outward. In the paper this produced two camps near 0 and 1.

steps.say: Start with a wide window: 0.3 on each side, a total of 0.6, the paper's own case. With no lean, the people at the ends feel one-sided influence and step inward by 0.15. That inward pull is what brings this crowd to consensus.

Now let people lean toward their own side: the further up you sit, the further up you look. The paper calls the strength of this lean the bias slope m. Because its direction depends on where you stand, it is an opinion-dependent bias.

The marked person at 0.7 now looks up about 0.35 and down about 0.25. The total is still 0.6, just shifted upward. More of what they hear lies above them, so they take a small step up, away from the middle.
Raise the lean further. The inward step at the ends shrinks, because each end person now looks mostly outward, where nobody is.
At full lean, the person at the very top looks only upward and finds no one above. Their inward step is zero, so they stay put. The paper saw exactly this in its run with a very strong lean.
Now compare the two curves. The dashed one, with no lean, pulls the ends inward. The solid one is positive above the middle and negative below it, so almost everyone moves outward.

The twist: this window was wide enough to agree, yet a person at 0.3 now steps down toward 0. Leaning to your own side turns the pull to the centre into a drift outward, and the crowd splits into two camps at the extremes.

understand.explanation: Earlier, the ends of the crowd felt only one-sided influence and were pulled inward, and that inward pull is what brought a wide-window crowd together. Now each person's window leans toward their own side. The total width stays the same, but people above the middle look further up and people below look further down, and the further out they sit, the stronger the lean. As the lean m grows, the people at the ends look mostly outward, where there is no one, so the inward pull fades and at m = 1 disappears. Meanwhile people nearer the middle see more views on their own side and drift outward. The paper simulated this with a total window of 0.6 (our ε = 0.3). Consensus held for a mild lean but broke down at about m ≈ 0.4, and stronger leans gave sharper polarisation, with the camps further apart. These are results from a simulated model in which everyone has the same window, not observations of real groups. Our picture also shows only the first round of an infinitely large, evenly spread crowd.
understand.quote: Thus, instead of a drive direction centre the opinion based bias generates a drift to the extremes.

check.task: Someone claims that a wide enough window always pulls everyone toward the middle. Prove them wrong: with a window at least as wide as the paper's 0.6 case, put the marked person below the middle and make them step away from the middle in round one.
check.hint: Widening the window alone keeps pulling people inward. Something else has to change, and the marked person must sit in the lower half, not too close to 0.
check.misconception: A wide enough listening window always guarantees consensus, whatever else people do.

connect.caption: This is the paper's rule for the lean. β_{r} is the share of the window pointing up (to the right) for a person at opinion x, and m is the slope of the lean. At m = 0 the split is half and half. At x = 0.5 it is always half and half, whatever m is. The paper's ε is the total window, so it equals 2 × the ε slider here: ε_{r} matches 'How far the marked person looks up' and ε_{l} matches 'How far the marked person looks down'.

concepts.recap: When people lean toward their own side, the ends stop moving in and the middle drifts out, so even a window wide enough for agreement can end in two extreme camps.
